chunks.section: LoRA’s Second Descent Extends Beyond Parameter Parity
chunks.text: Yueran Ma Affiliation: The University of Queensland Affiliation: Brisbane, Australia Email: s4931778@student.uq.edu.au

Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

A practitioner fine-tuning a pretrained backbone on a few thousand possibly mislabeled examples has a capacity dial to set, the rank r r of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , and double descent tells them which way to turn it. As capacity grows, test risk follows the classical U-shape, peaks near the interpolation threshold where the model first fits the training data exactly, and then descends again, so that the largest interpolating models often generalize best ( Belkin et al., 2019 ; Nakkiran et al., 2020 ; Spigler et al., 2019 ) . Label noise, the very condition that makes rank selection worth worrying about, amplifies the peak ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) . Applied to the rank axis, the advice is counterintuitive and actionable: once past the peak, raise the rank. Whether the rank axis obeys that advice has not been measured. Prior work documents task-dependent rank optima, degradation at high rank, reduced memorization under low-rank updates, and theoretical analyses of rank ( Jung et al., 2025 ; Rathore et al., 2025 ; Steele, 2026 ; Park, 2026 ; Zindari et al., 2026 ; Bossy et al., 2026 ) , and double descent has been analyzed in linear and deep transfer learning ( Dar & Baraniuk, 2022 ; Dar et al., 2022 ) . None combines an operational interpolation threshold on the rank axis, risk measurements past the expressivity limit r = d r{=}d (the model width, at which the adapter can first express any dense update), and a comparison of the tail with the same modules trained densely. The sweep range and the dense reference decide the answer.

The shape, and where sweeps stop. Sweeping rank on an ImageNet-pretrained DeiT-Tiny under label noise, we find test risk minimized at r = 1 r{=}1 , climbing steeply exactly as ranks acquire the ability to fit the noisy labels, and peaking well below full rank. We call this shape the interpolation cliff (Figure 1 ). What matters for measuring the axis is where sweeps conventionally end. Stopped at full rank, the axis has undone 0.033 0.033 of the 0.531 0.531 nats the peak cost and reads as a flat plateau. When the sweep extends to 4 ​ d 4d , risk keeps descending. Whether a sweep sees the second descent depends on how far it is allowed to run (Section 3 ). Figure 1: Two shapes, and why the reference point decides between them. (a) On a from-scratch capacity axis, risk peaks at interpolation and then descends past its own pre-peak valley, the only reference such an axis has. (b) On an adapter’s rank axis a second reference exists, dense fine-tuning of the same modules. Parity, the rank at which the adapter has as many trainable weights as dense fine-tuning, arrives before r = d r{=}d , the smallest rank that can express every dense update, so the adapter stops saving parameters before it is as expressive as dense. Schematic; measurements in Figure 2 .

A protocol that sets the reference point. “How much of the peak was undone” has no answer without a reference, and this axis offers two that disagree. Grading the tail against the sweep’s own valley is what the double-descent literature does, because a from-scratch width sweep has no unrestricted counterpart to compare against. An adapter axis has one. The module-matched rank sweep (MMRS) runs the dial past full rank and grades every point against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules, sharing seeds, subsets and noise draws, with the trainable-parameter ratio reported beside every risk difference (Section 4 ). On this family the two references have room to disagree, because the window in which the adapter saves parameters closes at parity, r = 0.75 ​ d r{=}0.75d , before it can express every dense update at r = d r{=}d (Figure 1 b).

What the tail costs. Under MMRS the descent is real and its price is legible. Every measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters has higher test negative log-likelihood (NLL) than dense, in every seed at a shared learning rate, so the descent becomes competitive with dense only after the adapter has stopped being cheaper than what it replaces. DeiT-Tiny first meets an equivalence margin of 0.05 0.05 nats at r = 3 ​ d r{=}3d , four times dense’s projection-weight count, and that result rests on one shared learning rate. The cheap end is a different matter: r = 1 r{=}1 leads dense by 0.40 0.40 and 0.27 0.27 nats on DeiT-Tiny and ViT-Tiny using 0.007 × 0.007\times dense’s projection-weight count, by far the largest risk reduction per added parameter. Qwen2.5-7B remains above dense at every measured rank while falling below its own pre-peak valley, so the two references answer the same sweep differently (Section 5.3 ). Since full rank supplies the expressivity, the remaining gap is not a function-class deficit; freezing one factor and controlling its spectrum isolates a condition-number effect on risk that disappears when the optimizer operates in update space (Section 5.4 ).

Double descent. The risk peak at interpolation and its subsequent descent were established by Belkin et al. (2019) , Spigler et al. (2019) and Advani et al. (2020) , extended to deep networks, epochs and data by Nakkiran et al. (2020) , and analyzed precisely in linear and random-features models ( Hastie et al., 2022 ; Mei & Montanari, 2022 ; Bartlett et al., 2020 ) , as reviewed by Belkin (2021) . Label noise amplifies the peak ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) , regularization can suppress it ( Nakkiran et al., 2021 ) , and related structure includes triple descent ( d’Ascoli et al., 2020 ) and grokking ( Power et al., 2022 ; Davies et al., 2023 ) . Nearest to our phenomenon, Xue et al. (2024) report a “final ascent” in the widest models once the noise-to-sample ratio is large, a regime our from-scratch transformer reproduces and our ResNet controls do not (Section 5.6 ). Closest in spirit to our diagnosis, Curth et al. (2023) argue that double descent hinges on what the capacity axis measures and Schaeffer et al. (2023) isolate the ingredients producing the peak. In transfer learning, Dar & Baraniuk (2022) analyze linear transfer and Dar et al. (2022) sweep frozen-layer count, neither along adapter rank.

LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) builds on intrinsic-dimension measurements of objective landscapes ( Li et al., 2018 ; Aghajanyan et al., 2021 ) ; its rank expressivity is characterized by Zeng & Lee (2024) and its scaling conventions by Kalajdzievski (2023) . That large ranks can hurt is established: accuracy stagnates past ranks of 32 32 – 64 64 ( Jung et al., 2025 ) , optima are task-dependent ( Rathore et al., 2025 ) , LoRA “learns less and forgets less” ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank updates memorize less in large language models ( Bossy et al., 2026 ) ; in noisy-label classification, Kim et al. (2024) find that the capacity limit of PEFT also impedes learning clean examples. Under label noise, theory places the optimal rank lower as noise grows ( Steele, 2026 ) and accuracy degrades with rank when noise is strong ( Zindari et al., 2026 ) , while Park (2026) and Rushka & Klabjan (2026) analyze rank sufficiency and approximation error. Empirically, Dennis et al. (2026) find ranks 16 16 to 128 128 all trailing full fine-tuning and Albert et al. (2025) ask whether the shortfall is parameters or rank, neither under label noise. These establish the two endpoints. What remains unmeasured is the shape between them, where risk peaks relative to the rank at which optimization interpolates, and whether the post-peak branch recovers once the adapter can express any dense update.

Effective capacity and optimization geometry. That LoRA’s update carries a stable rank well below its nominal rank is likewise established, as a pathology to engineer away ( Lion et al., 2025 ) and as a sweep locating where validation accuracy turns ( Awofeso et al., 2025 ) ; we add its placement relative to interpolation and an intervention on it. Parameterization matters beyond expressivity ( Shuttleworth et al., 2025 ) , and learning rate interacts with rank through initialization and scaling ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , which is why the shared-rate sweep is checked against per-arm rates (each at its own rate) on every backbone (Section 5.3 , Appendices C.2 and C.3 ). The optimization geometry of the factored parameterization is mapped: freezing one factor ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ) or both ( Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) , preconditioning the gradient ( Zhang & Pilanci, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Ghosh et al., 2026 ) , and showing that different factorizations of one Δ ​ W \Delta W converge differently ( Castin et al., 2026 ; Oh et al., 2026 ) . Those results concern training and generalization of the factorization; ours concern where the post-peak branch reaches dense risk (Section 5.3 ). Chang et al. (2025) use “double descent” for a transient training-loss divergence, a different object. Memorization and calibration under noise. Interpolating noisy labels forces memorization ( Zhang et al., 2017 ; Feldman & Zhang, 2020 ) , and calibration itself depends on overparameterization in high-dimensional models ( Clarté et al., 2023 ) , which is why we separate the risk we measure from the temperature it is read at (Section 5.6 ).

Unless noted, this section uses an ImageNet-pretrained DeiT-Tiny on 5 5 k-example CIFAR-100 subsets with 20 % 20\% symmetric label noise and LoRA on the fused query-key-value (qkv) projections of the last six blocks (full protocol in Section 5.1 ). Risk rises where the adapter begins to fit noise. Test NLL is minimized at r = 1 r{=}1 , below that of the linear probe, so a single rank of adaptation already beats frozen features. The curve then climbs steeply and peaks at r = 64 r{=}64 , 0.53 0.53 nats above the minimum (Figure 2 a). Train accuracy locates the climb: it crosses 99 % 99\% between r = 16 r{=}16 and r = 24 r{=}24 , so risk rises exactly as ranks acquire the ability to fit the noisy training set within budget (Figure 5 ). With clean labels the shape flattens into a mild monotone rise; label noise amplifies this peak as it does the classical one ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) . Where classical double descent would begin descending, the noisy curve instead keeps rising to r = 64 r{=}64 , and accuracy tells the same story, still below its rank-one level at r = 4 ​ d r{=}4d (Table 8 ). The pipeline does produce textbook double descent. From-scratch ResNet-18 width sweeps, run with the same data loading, noise injection, optimizer family and evaluation, peak in the interior and then carry risk below their own pre-peak valley, by 0.196 0.196 nats on CIFAR-10 and, on the identical CIFAR-100 subsets used for fine-tuning, by 0.658 0.658 nats, in every seed on both datasets (Figure 7 ). Dataset, sample size and noise draw are not what slows the second descent.

Counting parameters says nothing about either landmark. Three thresholds that classical linear accounts implicitly align come apart here (Figure 5 ): the smallest rank whose trainable-parameter count reaches n n , the smallest whose train accuracy reaches 99 % 99\% , and the rank of maximal risk. The first threshold is already passed at r = 0 r{=}0 , since even the linear head has more trainable parameters than there are training examples. The second arrives at r = 24 r{=}24 and the third at r = 64 r{=}64 . Raw parameter count is uninformative about both landmarks, a sharp PEFT instance of the parameter-counting critique ( Curth et al., 2023 ) ; interpolation here has to be measured, not counted. The conventional sweep range hides the far side. Stopped at r = d r{=}d the tail reads as a flat plateau; extended to 4 ​ d 4d the same curve keeps descending (Figure 2 b). Whether a sweep shows the second descent depends on its range, the first thing a protocol has to pin down. The other is the reference point, and this axis supplies two.

Problem statement. Let a pretrained network carry modules ℳ \mathcal{M} with frozen weights W m ∈ ℝ p × d W_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d} . A parameter-efficient family assigns to each setting r r of a capacity dial a set of admissible updates Δ ​ W ∈ 𝒰 ⁡ ( r ) ⊆ ℝ p × d \Delta W\in\mathcal{U}(r)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p\times d} , nested so that 𝒰 ⁡ ( r ) ⊆ 𝒰 ⁡ ( r ′ ) \mathcal{U}(r)\subseteq\mathcal{U}(r^{\prime}) whenever r < r ′ r<r^{\prime} . Nothing below uses more than nestedness. Let R ⁡ ( r ) R(r) be expected test risk after training at setting r r on n n examples whose labels carry noise rate η \eta , let R dense R_{\mathrm{dense}} be the risk of training the same modules over all of ℝ p × d \mathbb{R}^{p\times d} , and let π ⁡ ( r ) \pi(r) be the trainable-parameter count at r r divided by the count for dense fine-tuning. With r peak = arg ⁡ max r ⁡ R ⁡ ( r ) r_{\mathrm{peak}}=\arg\max_{r}R(r) and r valley = arg ⁡ min r ≤ r peak ⁡ R ⁡ ( r ) r_{\mathrm{valley}}=\arg\min_{r\leq r_{\mathrm{peak}}}R(r) , a second descent on this axis is a claim about R R for r > r peak r>r_{\mathrm{peak}} , and two quantities make it precise: Rec ⁡ ( r ) = R ⁡ ( r peak ) − R ⁡ ( r ) R ⁡ ( r peak ) − R ⁡ ( r valley ) , G ⁡ ( r ) = R ⁡ ( r ) − R dense . \mathrm{Rec}(r)\;=\;\frac{R(r_{\mathrm{peak}})-R(r)}{R(r_{\mathrm{peak}})-R(r_{\mathrm{valley}})},\qquad\qquad G(r)\;=\;R(r)-R_{\mathrm{dense}}. (1)

The first grades the tail against the sweep’s own valley, so Rec = 1 \mathrm{Rec}{=}1 is a return to it and Rec > 1 \mathrm{Rec}{>}1 an overshoot; the second grades it against the same modules trained without the restriction to 𝒰 ⁡ ( r ) \mathcal{U}(r) . On a from-scratch capacity axis, the restriction is the model, so no unrestricted counterpart exists. Only Rec \mathrm{Rec} is available, which is why recoveries are read against a valley in the double-descent literature. An adapter axis supplies both, and they can disagree without contradiction, since a sweep may drive Rec \mathrm{Rec} above one while G G remains positive at every setting with π ⁡ ( r ) < 1 \pi(r)<1 . A second descent certified by Rec \mathrm{Rec} alone can therefore be one that matches dense only where π ⁡ ( r ) ≥ 1 \pi(r)\geq 1 . Where the axis changes character. Two settings organize the tail. The expressivity limit r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} is the smallest r r with 𝒰 ⁡ ( r ) = ℝ p × d \mathcal{U}(r)=\mathbb{R}^{p\times d} ; below it the dial enlarges the function class, above it only the parameterization grows redundant, so a descent past r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} is a descent under redundancy rather than classical capacity-driven double descent. The parity point r parity r_{\mathrm{parity}} is the smallest r r with π ⁡ ( r ) ≥ 1 \pi(r)\geq 1 , past which the family has stopped being parameter-efficient at all. For LoRA on modules of different shapes, r expr = max m ⁡ min ⁡ ( p m , d m ) r_{\mathrm{expr}}=\max_{m}\min(p_{m},d_{m}) , since the update class is full only once every module’s update class is full, while r parity r_{\mathrm{parity}} is set by the total count.

Nothing forces an order on these two, and for LoRA the order is the unhelpful one. A rank- r r adapter on a p × d p\times d projection trains r ⁡ ( p + d ) r(p+d) weights against dense’s p ​ d pd , so r parity = p ​ d / ( p + d ) r_{\mathrm{parity}}=pd/(p+d) while r expr = min ⁡ ( p , d ) r_{\mathrm{expr}}=\min(p,d) . A fused qkv projection has p = 3 ​ d p=3d , giving r parity = 3 4 ​ d < d = r expr . r_{\mathrm{parity}}\;=\;\tfrac{3}{4}d\;\;<\;\;d\;=\;r_{\mathrm{expr}}. (2) The parameter-saving window closes before the adapter can express every dense update. Any recovery that arrives after r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} therefore lies past parity, where an adapter no longer saves parameters. This is why G G and π \pi have to be read together. Interpolation is located, not counted. The operational interpolation threshold r interp ​ ( T ) r_{\mathrm{interp}}(T) is the smallest r r whose mean train accuracy reaches 99 % 99\% within a training budget T T . Exceeding n n trainable parameters, the counting threshold, does not confer interpolation, because a head linear in frozen features is constrained by the feature geometry, not its parameter count. Classical accounts align both thresholds with r peak r_{\mathrm{peak}} ; a protocol on this axis has to report the three separately.

Protocol. MMRS combines five choices. (i) Extend the sweep to a multiple of r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} rather than stopping at it. (ii) Train dense on exactly ℳ \mathcal{M} , sharing seeds, subsets and noise draws with every adapter arm, and report paired per-seed differences. (iii) Report G ⁡ ( r ) G(r) with π ⁡ ( r ) \pi(r) beside it and mark r parity r_{\mathrm{parity}} on the axis, so no risk gain is read without its parameter price. (iv) Hold the learning rate fixed across arms for the paired sweep, so a per-seed difference reflects the update class rather than the schedule. Then check that per-arm rates do not reverse the ordering, selecting each arm’s rate on some seeds and scoring the pair on others; a shared rate can favor whichever arm it suits ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and a rate scored on the seeds that selected it flatters the higher-variance arm. (v) Locate r interp r_{\mathrm{interp}} from train accuracy at the budget in use and r peak r_{\mathrm{peak}} from test risk, and report both.

After the shared setup, we read the sweep from its cheap end (Section 5.2 ) through the tail graded against dense (Section 5.3 ) to what separates the two arms at full rank (Section 5.4 ), and then ask whether the cliff belongs to LoRA and how robust its diagnosis is (Sections 5.5 and 5.6 ).

Task and backbones. In the main testbed, we fine-tune an ImageNet-1k-pretrained DeiT-Tiny ( Touvron et al., 2021 ; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ; Wightman, 2019 ) of width d = 192 d{=}192 on class-balanced subsets of CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) with n = 5,000 n{=}5{,}000 training examples. A fraction η \eta of training labels is resampled uniformly among the other classes ( 20 % 20\% unless stated). Evaluation uses the untouched 10 10 k test set. The primary metric is test NLL, the risk addressed by double-descent theory and a more sensitive measure than 0 0 – 1 1 loss, with accuracy and calibrated variants reported alongside it. Each comparison with dense is reported as G ⁡ ( r ) G(r) from Equation 1 , which is negative when the adapter has lower risk, with π ⁡ ( r ) \pi(r) beside it. Bracketed values are 95 % 95\% bootstrap intervals over paired seeds and are descriptive when only three seeds are shared.

Adapter axis. We wrap the fused qkv projections of the last six transformer blocks with LoRA, so that W ​ x → W ​ x + s ​ B ​ A ​ x Wx\rightarrow Wx+sBAx with A ∈ ℝ r × d A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} , B ∈ ℝ 3 ​ d × r B\in\mathbb{R}^{3d\times r} , and B B initialized to zero. The base layer is frozen. Unless stated otherwise, we use s = 1 s{=}1 ; Appendix E.1 covers α / r \alpha/r scaling and rsLoRA ( Kalajdzievski, 2023 ) . A freshly initialized linear head is always trained ( 19,300 19{,}300 parameters), and r = 0 r{=}0 denotes linear probing. Training uses AdamW ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019 ) at a shared learning rate of 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} for 40 40 epochs by default, with 5 5 seeds for the main sweep; the remaining settings are in Appendix A . Seeds control the subset, noise draw and initialization. Parameter ratios π ⁡ ( r ) \pi(r) compare trainable projection weights, excluding the common head; the vision dense arm also trains the qkv biases, which full-rank updates can absorb on the frozen LayerNorm outputs (Appendix D.1 ). From-scratch controls. We train ResNet-18 ( He et al., 2016 ) from scratch with the same pipeline across widths, on noisy CIFAR-10 and on the CIFAR-100 subsets used for fine-tuning, with 3 3 seeds each (widths and budgets in Table 2 ).

chunks.section: 5.2 Rank one yields the most risk reduction per parameter
chunks.text: Measured as the NLL drop from the linear probe divided by the parameters added, the return of the first rank exceeds that of any other rank on the axis, on DeiT-Tiny, ViT-Tiny ( Steiner et al., 2022 ) and at 7 7 B. A single rank of adaptation also leads module-matched dense fine-tuning by 0.400 0.400 nats on DeiT-Tiny, 0.272 0.272 on ViT-Tiny and, at per-arm rates, 0.071 0.071 on Swin-Tiny ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , in every seed, using under one percent of dense’s projection-weight count (Table 1 , Appendices C.1 and C.2 ). On these three backbones r = 1 r{=}1 dominates dense outright, cheaper and lower-risk at once, and needs no argument about the tail. The domination is consistent with strong regularization at small rank. On DeiT-Small ( Touvron et al., 2021 ) and at 7 7 B the picture under the shared rate is a trade-off rather than a domination: dense attains the lowest risk, r = 1 r{=}1 comes within 0.074 0.074 and 0.061 0.061 nats of it on under one percent of its projection weights, and at 7 7 B every sampled rank from 448 448 to 900 900 falls between, lower-risk than r = 1 r{=}1 while still cheaper than dense (Appendices C.1 and C.3 ). These ranks are points on a cost–risk frontier that a practitioner with an intermediate budget may want. What none of them does is reach dense, which is what Section 5.3 measures.

chunks.section: 5.3 The parameter-saving window closes before the descent arrives
chunks.text: Every measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters carries higher risk than dense fine-tuning of the same projections, on DeiT-Tiny, ViT-Tiny and DeiT-Small, in every seed at a shared learning rate (Figure 2 b, Table 1 , Appendix C.1 ). The descent itself is genuine, since the DeiT-Tiny and ViT-Tiny sweeps keep falling past the peak once extended to 4 ​ d 4d ; what the paired column adds is its price, a gap that narrows only from above and only slowly, so wherever it closes at all it closes far outside the range where the adapter was still cheaper than dense. Inside the window. We sample five ranks between the peak and r parity r_{\mathrm{parity}} on DeiT-Tiny and three on ViT-Tiny, five seeds each, since those are the only points where a recovery could still retain a parameter advantage (Appendix C.1 ). None reaches dense. The paired gap remains between + 0.084 +0.084 and + 0.140 +0.140 nats, roughly four to seven times its seed-to-seed spread, and every seed agrees in sign on both NLL and accuracy. Giving each arm its own learning rate, selected on three seeds, narrows these gaps without closing them: re-run on ten fresh seeds, DeiT-Tiny’s r = 128 r{=}128 trails dense by + 0.062 +0.062 nats ( 95 % 95\% t t -interval [ + 0.026 , + 0.099 ] [+0.026,+0.099] , nine of ten seeds), and ViT-Tiny’s trails by + 0.065 +0.065 on every selection seed (Appendix C.2 ). We have measured the window in which a recovery could still match dense while saving parameters, and it is empty.

chunks.section: 5.3 The parameter-saving window closes before the descent arrives
chunks.text: Outside the window. At r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} , where either adapter can already express any dense weight update, both backbones remain behind dense. Under the shared rate, DeiT-Tiny passes a paired equivalence test with two one-sided tests (TOST) against a 0.05 0.05 -nat margin, a tenth of the cliff’s depth, first at r = 3 ​ d r{=}3d (eight seeds), four times dense’s projection-weight count; ViT-Tiny does not pass it there. With each arm at its own best rate, dense gains from a higher rate while LoRA’s best at 3 ​ d 3d is the shared one, so the difference there becomes + 0.031 +0.031 nats, positive in every seed but inside the margin (Appendix C.2 ); the equivalence at 3 ​ d 3d is established only under the shared rate. The same shortfall at 7 7 B. To test the finding at language-model scale, we repeat the measurement on Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) over 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples ( Zhang et al., 2015 ) with 20 % 20\% label noise, adapting the qkv projections of the last six blocks at twelve ranks up to d = 3584 d{=}3584 against dense fine-tuning of the same modules ( 3 3 shared seeds; Appendix C.3 ). Grouped-query attention makes the projections cheap relative to the adapter and places parity at r ≈ 1075 r{\approx}1075 , which we sample, so this axis is the clean test of the two references in Equation 1 . They part company sharply (Figure 3 ). At r = 448 r{=}448 the valley reference reads Rec = 1.06 \mathrm{Rec}{=}1.06 , a second descent that has already completed, while the dense reference puts the same point 0.058 0.058 nats short, and G G remains positive at every measured rank and in every seed, parity included. Read against a valley this sweep recovers fully; read against dense it never arrives.

chunks.section: 5.3 The parameter-saving window closes before the descent arrives
5.4 Optimization coordinates change risk inside a fixed update class
chunks.text: The residual gap at full rank is not a shortage of expressivity. Since 𝒰 ⁡ ( r ) = ℝ p × d \mathcal{U}(r)=\mathbb{R}^{p\times d} for r ≥ r expr r\geq r_{\mathrm{expr}} , the adapter and dense search the same set from r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} upward, so any risk difference there stems from how the search is parameterized rather than from what it can reach. The interventions below hold the update class fixed and vary the coordinates, showing that coordinates alone can move risk by roughly the size of the gap. Which property of the coordinates produces the gap in ordinary LoRA, where both factors train jointly, remains open. Figure 4: Risk changes with optimization coordinates. We compare ordinary LoRA and three interventions on DeiT-Tiny over the same three seeds. The ViT-Tiny results are in Appendix D . Different solutions at full rank. The learned updates differ even where the two procedures search the same set: LoRA’s update norm grows with rank while its stable rank, ‖ Δ ​ W ‖ F 2 / ‖ Δ ​ W ‖ 2 2 \|\Delta W\|_{F}^{2}/\|\Delta W\|_{2}^{2} , lags far behind nominal rank, and dense reaches a higher stable rank with a smaller norm, a broader spectrum (Appendix D.1 ). Reaching the same function class does not mean reaching the same solution.

chunks.section: 5.4 Optimization coordinates change risk inside a fixed update class
chunks.text: Freezing one factor changes the tail. Holding A A fixed makes B ↦ B ​ A B\mapsto BA linear while preserving the full weight-update class at r ≥ d r\geq d . Frozen-factor methods already use this construction ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ) ; here we choose the spectrum of A A to control the coordinates. With an orthonormal draw the adapter ends 0.012 0.012 nats above dense at r = d r{=}d and 0.005 0.005 below it at 2 ​ d 2d , on the same three seeds (Figure 4 ). Only B B is trained, with 3 ​ d ​ r 3dr projection weights, so its weight count matches dense’s at r = d r{=}d and is twice dense’s at 2 ​ d 2d . At r = d r{=}d the orthonormal map is an isometry; for r > d r>d , A ⊤ ​ A = I A^{\top}A=I and the map remains surjective, with redundant directions in B B . Prescribing the condition number κ ⁡ ( A ) ∈ { 1 , 3 , 5 } \kappa(A)\in\{1,3,5\} at r = 2 ​ d r{=}2d then keeps the update class fixed while raising risk monotonically in κ \kappa , with stable rank falling in step, on both backbones (Figure 4 , Table 6 ). Risk depends on the spectrum of a factor that cannot change what the adapter can express. Below parity, freezing A A also improves on ordinary LoRA at every tested rank above the valley, by 0.025 0.025 – 0.072 0.072 nats on DeiT-Tiny and 0.052 0.052 on ViT-Tiny, yet both frozen arms still finish above dense at r = 128 r{=}128 , their largest tested rank below parity.

chunks.section: 5.4 Optimization coordinates change risk inside a fixed update class
chunks.text: Optimizing in update space removes the condition-number effect. With A A frozen, ∇ B ℒ = ∇ Δ ​ W ℒ ​ A ⊤ \nabla_{B}\mathcal{L}=\nabla_{\Delta W}\mathcal{L}\,A^{\top} . A gradient-descent step on B B therefore multiplies the update-space gradient by A ⊤ ​ A A^{\top}A . AdamW further scales each coordinate through its moment estimates. We keep those estimates directly on Δ ​ W \Delta W and lift each step back to B B through a left inverse of A A . This construction makes the update-space step independent of the chosen factor spectrum. The spectrum then stops mattering. The paired NLL difference between κ = 5 \kappa{=}5 and κ = 1 \kappa{=}1 collapses from 0.065 0.065 nats to under 10 − 4 10^{-4} on DeiT-Tiny and from 0.055 0.055 to under 10 − 3 10^{-3} on ViT-Tiny, each lifted arm lands within 0.003 0.003 nats of its dense reference, and stable rank rises to dense’s (Table 6 ). The effect of factor geometry on gradients and convergence is established ( Oh et al., 2026 ; Castin et al., 2026 ) ; these experiments show its consequence for test risk at a fixed update class. In ordinary LoRA, κ ⁡ ( A ) \kappa(A) ranges from 2.8 2.8 to 12.2 12.2 across r ∈ { 24 , … , 128 } r\in\{24,\ldots,128\} . Projecting A A to κ ⁡ ( A ) = 1 \kappa(A){=}1 after each step closes most of the full-rank gap, but a projection that preserves B ​ A BA gives higher risk at the same condition number (Appendix D.3 ), so κ ⁡ ( A ) \kappa(A) alone does not decide the gap. Stable rank is similarly incomplete: a scale-invariant penalty lifts it from 11.2 11.2 to 40.3 40.3 while recovering a tenth of the distance to the valley; at matched stable rank, dense remains 0.070 0.070 nats ahead.

chunks.section: 5.4 Optimization coordinates change risk inside a fixed update class
chunks.text: Test NLL tracks training NLL more closely than rank. Pooled over the 175 175 fixed-setting runs, test NLL correlates with train NLL at Spearman ρ = − 0.86 \rho{=}{-}0.86 and with nominal rank at only 0.40 0.40 , an ordering that persists after adjustment for the training budget, while higher rank lowers risk within most fully interpolated groups (Appendix D.4 ). How closely a run fits the noisy labels predicts its risk better than its rank does.

chunks.section: 5.5 Dense axes recover more of the same cliff
chunks.text: To test whether the cliff is specific to LoRA or to one backbone, we sweep two dense capacity axes, a second PEFT family and three further backbones. The cliff is not an artifact of LoRA or of DeiT-Tiny, while both PEFT families recover less of it than the dense axes (Figures 9 and 10 b). Dense capacity axes climb the same cliff. Unfreezing the last k k blocks, or training only their qkv projections densely, produces a cliff deeper than LoRA’s from the same head-only start. Both then run a real second descent, recovering 0.474 0.474 and 0.395 0.395 nats of what their peaks cost, against 0.033 0.033 nats on the rank axis by r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} . At k = 6 k{=}6 the module-matched arm trains the same projections as LoRA and finishes about 0.10 0.10 nats below the full-rank adapter, a gap of the size that coordinates alone can produce (Section 5.4 ). A second PEFT family has the flattest tail. Houlsby-style bottleneck adapters ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) on the last six blocks, with bottleneck width m m as the capacity axis, trace the full shape from a valley at m = 1 m{=}1 through a peak, then dip by 0.016 0.016 nats of a 0.727 0.727 -nat cliff even past twice the model width. Restricted-update families, not LoRA specifically, are what flatten the far side.

chunks.section: 5.5 Dense axes recover more of the same cliff
chunks.text: The rank-one valley holds across backbones. We test three further backbones with data, noise, optimizer and budget held fixed, each with a module-matched dense arm (Appendix C.1 ), and two things persist across all of them: the pre-peak valley sits at r = 1 r{=}1 , and every other sampled rank inside the parameter-saving window finishes above that valley. ViT-Tiny replicates the cliff in full despite sharing neither recipe nor pretraining data, and remains above dense at every sampled post-peak rank (Table 1 ). DeiT-Small has a far shallower cliff and, at 2.7 × 2.7\times dense’s parameters, finishes below its valley at 2 ​ d 2d in every seed; against dense it still trails at r = 192 r{=}192 , below parity, and at 2 ​ d 2d , by + 0.129 +0.129 and + 0.032 +0.032 nats under the shared rate and by + 0.056 +0.056 and + 0.040 +0.040 at per-arm rates, in every seed. Swin-Tiny has no cliff. Its risk rises monotonically from r = 1 r{=}1 , which already interpolates and is still the valley, so the rise tracks capacity added past the valley rather than the crossing of interpolation, and there the cheap end wins. At the shared rate, dense overfits and finishes above the linear probe; at each arm’s own rate, where all three arms stop short of interpolation, r = 1 r{=}1 and r = 384 r{=}384 still beat dense in every seed, by 0.071 0.071 and 0.055 0.055 nats (Appendix C.2 ).

The rise is not (mostly) miscalibration. Fitting a temperature on a held-out clean split never used for training ( Guo et al., 2017 ) leaves 83 % 83\% of the noisy cliff standing ( 0.44 0.44 vs. 0.53 0.53 nats, 5 5 seeds), rescaling leaves the accuracy drop unchanged, and expected calibration error, Brier score and selective-risk area all degrade across the same range ( Naeini et al., 2015 ; Brier, 1950 ; Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017 ; Geifman et al., 2019 ) . With clean labels calibration removes about half the rise instead (Table 12 ). Under label noise, the cliff is mostly real error rather than overconfidence. Noise and augmentation change only the cliff’s depth. CIFAR-100N human re-annotation labels ( Wei et al., 2022 ) replicate the cliff with larger amplitude. Sweeping η ∈ { 10 , 20 , 40 , 60 } % \eta\in\{10,20,40,60\}\% keeps the valley pinned at r = 1 r{=}1 while the amplitude grows monotonically, and augmentation shrinks the amplitude without changing the shape or adding a second descent (Appendix E.1 ). The peak moves with the training budget. From 40 40 to 80 80 epochs it shifts from r = 64 r{=}64 to r = 32 r{=}32 , and at 20 20 epochs risk is monotone in rank because low ranks have not yet interpolated. The peak reflects interpolation status at the current budget ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) , so the protocol locates r interp r_{\mathrm{interp}} per budget. Neither longer training nor α / r \alpha/r scaling returns the tail to the valley (Appendix B.1 ).

Model selection shrinks the cliff without removing it. Selecting learning rate, weight decay and stopping epoch on a clean validation split reduces the cliff from 0.53 0.53 to 0.16 0.16 nats. The selected models retain the rank ordering on fresh seeds, and every selected checkpoint precedes interpolation (Appendix E.2 ), which is the mechanism: selection escapes the cliff by declining to interpolate, not by crossing it. Because per-rank selection includes no dense arm, it bears on the shape of the axis and not on the gap to dense. No tested setting removes the cliff once ranks interpolate. Corrupting the frozen backbone only deepens the cliff, and its shape persists through changes in data size, learning rate, weight decay, scaling, adapter placement and dataset (Appendices C.2 , E.1 and E.3 ; Table 15 ). Architecture decides too. A ResNet completes the descent on these subsets; a width-scaled ViT trained from scratch does not (Appendix B.2 ), recovering 0.56 0.56 of 3.23 3.23 nats, the final-ascent regime of Xue et al. (2024) . Dense-block fine-tuning of a transformer reaches Rec = 0.82 \mathrm{Rec}{=}0.82 , so the rank axis’s shallow far side is not a transformer property. Scope. The experiments cover noisy image and text classification with AdamW, synthetic and human label noise, and budgets up to 160 160 epochs. The dense reference is module-matched, training the projections LoRA adapts rather than the whole network; the dense-block axis of Section 5.5 unfreezes up to six full blocks. Test NLL is the primary measurement, and accuracy follows its ordering inside the parameter-saving window but can diverge at larger ranks. Where LoRA crosses dense depends on the protocol and the grid.

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.

Data. CIFAR-100/CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) images are upsampled bilinearly to 224 2 224^{2} and normalized with ImageNet statistics (ViT-Tiny uses the 0.5 0.5 normalization of its checkpoint). Subsets are class-balanced ( n / C n/C per class over C C classes, selected by seed-controlled RNG). Symmetric label noise resamples a fraction η \eta of training labels uniformly among the remaining C − 1 C-1 classes; the noise pattern is seed-controlled and identical across ranks within a seed. No data augmentation is used in the main sweeps (isolating the capacity axis); E23 repeats the noisy rank sweep with random flip, pad-and-crop ( 16 16 px at 224 2 224^{2} scale, one offset shared per batch), and mixup ( α = 0.2 \alpha{=}0.2 ). Models. We use DeiT-Tiny ( 5.7 5.7 M parameters, patch 16 16 , width 192 192 ) and DeiT-Small ( Touvron et al., 2021 ) from timm ( Wightman, 2019 ) with ImageNet-1k pretrained weights; the classification head is replaced by a freshly initialized linear layer. ViT-Tiny and Swin-Tiny are described in Table 14 , and Qwen2.5-7B in Appendix C.3 . LoRA wraps the fused qkv linear layers of the last six blocks; A A is initialized with Kaiming-uniform values and B B with zeros, so training starts at the pretrained function. The scaling schemes are fixed ( s = 1 s=1 ), standard ( s = α / r s=\alpha/r , α = 16 \alpha=16 ), and rsLoRA ( Kalajdzievski, 2023 , s = α / r s=\alpha/\sqrt{r} , α = 16 \alpha=16 ;) . In E15, LoRA adapts the fused c_attn projection of the last six blocks of GPT-2 ( Radford et al., 2019 ) ; training runs for 12 12 epochs at lr 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} on 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples with 20 % 20\% label noise, and there is no dense arm.

Training. We train with AdamW (lr 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} unless swept, wd 10 − 2 10^{-2} , cosine annealing to 0 0 , batch 64 64 ) and bfloat16 autocast for 40 40 epochs unless stated. Each run logs train/test NLL and accuracy every 5 5 epochs, final per-example test logits, and per-layer stable ranks of the update. Calibration protocol. Temperature is fit by grid/LBFGS on a class-balanced 5 5 k split drawn from the training pool, disjoint from the training subset, with true labels (clean); test labels are never used for fitting. chunks.section: Appendix F A minimal warm-start linear model
chunks.text: A warm-start linear model isolates how prior quality changes the height of the valley relative to the interpolating tail. For p > n p>n and a nonzero prior error or noise variance, the expression increases with k k , placing the pre-interpolation valley at the smallest subspace dimension.
